Test your Soroban contracts in a local sandbox environment before deploying to testnet. This guide covers the complete local development workflow — from unit tests and CLI sandbox invocation to state inspection and debugging loops.
Soroban CLI installed (stellar --version) Contract project initialized or use the counter example from this repo Rust toolchain with wasm32-unknown-unknown target

The local testing loop follows this flow: Write/Edit Code → Build → Run Tests → Inspect State → Fix → Repeat ↓ Deploy to Testnet Every iteration happens entirely on your machine — no network connection, no testnet funds, no waiting for ledgers.
Soroban contracts compile to native code during cargo test, giving you fast feedback without WASM compilation.

Every test starts with a sandbox Env: #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::Env; #[test] fn test_initial_value() { let env = Env::default(); // fresh sandbox let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); // deploy in sandbox let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); } } Env::default() creates a sandbox with a simulated ledger. Contracts registered here exist only in memory — no network involved.

# Run all tests cargo test # Run a specific test cargo test test_initial_value # Run tests with stdout output visible cargo test -- --nocapture # Run tests single-threaded (useful when debugging) cargo test -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture

Test sequences of operations and verify state after each step: #[test] fn test_increment_sequence() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 1); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 2); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 3); assert_eq!(client.get(), 3); // read-only check client.reset(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); // verify reset } Each test gets its own isolated Env — state from one test never leaks into another.
Beyond unit tests, the Soroban CLI provides a sandbox mode that invokes your compiled WASM locally, giving you the same execution path that runs on testnet.
First, build the optimised WASM artifact: stellar contract build

Use --local to run against the local sandbox instead of a network: stellar contract invoke \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter.optimized.wasm \ --local \ -- increment Expected output: 1 Each --local invocation starts with a fresh sandbox. State is not persisted between calls.

Aspect --local sandbox --network testnet Network required No Yes Fees charged No Yes (testnet XLM) State persists Per invocation Indefinitely Speed Instant ~3-5 seconds per ledger Ideal for Iterative development Final validation

Chain operations to simulate a real session: # Increment multiple times stellar contract invoke \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter.optimized.wasm \ --local \ -- increment stellar contract invoke \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter.optimized.wasm \ --local \ -- increment # Read current value stellar contract invoke \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter.optimized.wasm \ --local \ -- get

Verify the contract interface before deploying: stellar contract inspect \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/counter.optimized.wasm Expected output: Functions: increment() -> u32 get() -> u32 reset() -> ()

Use println! in tests and run with --nocapture: #[test] fn test_with_debug_output() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let result = client.increment(); println!("After increment: {}", result); let state = client.get(); println!("Current state: {}", state); assert_eq!(state, 1); } cargo test test_with_debug_output -- --nocapture

Emit events in your contract to trace execution: use soroban_sdk::{symbol_short, Symbol}; pub fn increment(env: Env) -> u32 { let count = env.storage().instance() .get(&symbol_short!("count")) .unwrap_or(0); let new_count = count + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("count"), &new_count); // Emit event for observability env.events().publish( (symbol_short!("increment"),), new_count, ); new_count } In tests, inspect emitted events: #[test] fn test_events_emitted() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); let events = env.events().all(); assert_eq!(events.len(), 1); let (contract, topics, data) = &events[0]; assert_eq!(*contract, contract_id); assert_eq!(topics, &(symbol_short!("increment"),).into_val(&env)); assert_eq!(data, 1_u32.into_val(&env)); }
When a test panics, get the full backtrace: RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo test For debug builds of the contract itself, use RUST_BACKTRACE=full: RUST_BACKTRACE=full cargo test -- --nocapture

Automatically re-run tests when code changes: # Install cargo-watch cargo install cargo-watch # Auto-test on every save cargo watch -x test # Auto-test with output cargo watch -x "test -- --nocapture"

Read and verify contract storage directly from test code: #[test] fn test_storage_inspection() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); // Read storage directly let count: u32 = env.storage().instance() .get(&symbol_short!("count")) .unwrap_or(0); assert_eq!(count, 1); }

Create snapshot files to track state changes across test runs. The test_snapshots directory stores golden files: #[test] fn test_snapshot() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); // Snapshot the current state let snapshot = env.ledger().get(); // Compare against stored snapshot in test_snapshots/ } Soroban generates snapshot files under test_snapshots/ when SOROBAN_SNAPSHOT_DIR is set or using the testutils feature. This lets you diff state changes across commits.

For contracts with complex state, log the full storage at key points: fn dump_storage(env: &Env) { // This is a conceptual helper — actual keys depend on your contract let keys = vec![&env, symbol_short!("count")]; for key in keys.iter() { if let Some(val) = env.storage().instance().get(&key) { let value: u32 = val; println!(" {} = {:?}", key, value); } } }

Control ledger state to simulate different conditions: #[test] fn test_ledger_configuration() { let env = Env::default(); // Set specific ledger timestamp env.ledger().with_mut(|li| { li.timestamp = 1700000000; li.sequence_number = 100000; li.max_entry_ttl = 31104000; // ~1 year }); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); // Contract sees the configured ledger state // ... }

Soroban requires authorization for certain operations. In tests, use mock_all_auths() to bypass signature verification: #[test] fn test_authorized_operation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); env.mock_all_auths(); // Skip real signature checks // All authorization checks pass client.increment(); } For more granular control, mock specific auths: #[test] fn test_specific_auth() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let admin = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_auths(&[MockAuth { address: &admin, invoke: &MockAuthInvoke { contract: &contract_id, fn_name: "admin_operation", args: (admin.clone(),).into_val(&env), sub_invokes: &[], }, }]); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); // admin_operation(&admin) will succeed for this specific caller }

Generate and use multiple addresses to test multi-user scenarios: #[test] fn test_multi_user_scenario() { let env = Env::default(); env.mock_all_auths(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); let charlie = Address::generate(&env); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); // Alice and Bob interact independently client.increment(); client.increment(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 2); }

Set resource limits to simulate testnet constraints: #[test] fn test_with_budget() { let env = Env::default(); // Set CPU and memory limits matching testnet env.budget().reset_unlimited(); env.budget().set_cpu_limit(100_000_000); env.budget().set_memory_limit(100_000_000); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let result = client.try_increment(); assert!(result.is_ok()); // Check how much budget was consumed let cpu_remaining = env.budget().get_cpu_remaining(); println!("CPU remaining: {}", cpu_remaining); }
This end-to-end walkthrough demonstrates the full local development cycle.
stellar contract init my-counter && cd my-counter

src/lib.rs contains a basic increment contract. Replace it with: #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, symbol_short, Env, Symbol}; const COUNTER: Symbol = symbol_short!("count"); #[contract] pub struct Counter; #[contractimpl] impl Counter { pub fn increment(env: Env) -> u32 { let count: u32 = env.storage().instance() .get(&COUNTER) .unwrap_or(0); let new_count = count + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &new_count); env.events().publish((symbol_short!("inc"),), new_count); new_count } pub fn get(env: Env) -> u32 { env.storage().instance() .get(&COUNTER) .unwrap_or(0) } pub fn reset(env: Env) { env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &0_u32); } }

Add tests to src/lib.rs: #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::testutils::Events; use soroban_sdk::Env; #[test] fn test_initial_state() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); } #[test] fn test_increment() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 1); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 2); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 3); } #[test] fn test_reset() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); client.increment(); client.reset(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); } #[test] fn test_events() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); let events = env.events().all(); assert_eq!(events.len(), 1); let (id, topics, data) = &events[0]; assert_eq!(topics, &(symbol_short!("inc"),).into_val(&env)); assert_eq!(*data, 1_u32.into_val(&env)); } }

cargo test Expected output: running 4 tests test tests::test_events ... ok test tests::test_initial_state ... ok test tests::test_increment ... ok test tests::test_reset ... ok test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

Modify increment to accidentally return the old value: pub fn increment(env: Env) -> u32 { let count: u32 = env.storage().instance() .get(&COUNTER) .unwrap_or(0); let new_count = count + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER, &new_count); count // BUG: returning old value instead of new } Run tests: cargo test The test_increment test fails: test tests::test_increment ... FAILED failures: ---- tests::test_increment stdout ---- thread 'tests::test_increment' panicked at src/lib.rs:54:9: assertion `left == right` failed left: 0 right: 1 The test caught the regression instantly — no testnet deploy needed.

The main differences are: Local Testnet Env::default() sandbox Live Stellar testnet --local flag --network testnet --source <account> Zero fees Testnet XLM required No account needed Funded account required Instant execution ~3-5 second ledger closes Isolated per run Persistent state

This pattern demonstrates a complete basic token contract implementing three core operations: mint, transfer, and balance. It serves as the foundation for understanding token mechanics in Soroban before advancing to standardized token interfaces like SAC (Soroban Asset Contract). When to use Use this pattern to bootstrap a simple token system, understand state management for balances, and grasp authorization patterns. For production, consider using SAC or wrapping existing assets. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Basic familiarity with Soroban contracts and the soroban_sdk Understanding of Address types and authentication Implementation The contract manages a ledger mapping addresses to token balances using persistent storage. Three public functions allow minting tokens, querying balances, and transferring between accounts. Contract Running Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; /// Storage key for tracking token balances per address. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), } /// Error codes for token operations. #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, SelfTransfer = 3, } #[contract] pub struct TokenTransfer; #[contractimpl] impl TokenTransfer { /// Mint tokens to an address (for testing and bootstrapping). /// In production, restrict this to authorized minters. pub fn mint(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) { let key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &(current + amount)); } /// Query the token balance of an address. pub fn balance(env: Env, of: Address) -> i128 { let key = DataKey::Balance(of); env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0) } /// Transfer tokens from sender to recipient. /// Requires authorization from the sender address. pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Prevent self-transfer if from == to { return Err(Error::SelfTransfer); } // Check sender has sufficient balance let from_key = DataKey::Balance(from.clone()); let from_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&from_key).unwrap_or(0); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Perform transfer let to_key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let to_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&to_key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&from_key, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&to_key, &(to_balance + amount)); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; fn setup() -> (Env, TokenTransferClient<'static>) { let env = Env::default(); env.mock_all_auths(); let contract_id = env.register(TokenTransfer, ()); let client = TokenTransferClient::new(&env, &contract_id); (env, client) } #[test] fn test_mint_increases_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 500); } #[test] fn test_transfer_moves_tokens() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &1000); client.transfer(&alice, &bob, &400); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 600); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 400); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_insufficient_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &200); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 100); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 0); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_invalid_amount() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &0); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); } #[test] fn test_self_transfer_is_rejected() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &alice, &50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::SelfTransfer))); } #[test] fn test_initial_balance_is_zero() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 0); } } Run the example tests to verify the implementation: cd examples/token-transfer cargo test Expected output: 6 passing tests covering mint, transfer, balance, validation, and edge cases. Key Concepts Storage Model​ Balances are stored in persistent storage using the Balance(Address) enum variant as the key. This allows efficient lookups and updates without scanning the entire ledger. Authorization​ The transfer function calls from.require_auth() to ensure the transaction is signed by the sender. This prevents unauthorized token transfers. Error Handling​ Three error codes cover the main failure modes: InsufficientBalance: Sender doesn't have enough tokens InvalidAmount: Zero or negative amounts are rejected SelfTransfer: Transferring to yourself is a no-op and disallowed Minting​ The mint function bypasses authorization checks. In production, restrict minting to authorized parties using a minter role or ownership model. Security Considerations Unrestricted Minting: The current implementation allows anyone to mint tokens. Add access control using an admin address or authorized minters list before production use. No Decimal Support: This basic implementation uses integers only. For real assets, consider implementing a decimals field and decimal-aware math. Supply Cap: Consider implementing a maximum supply to prevent unlimited inflation. Allowance/Approval: For more advanced use cases, implement an approve/transferFrom pattern allowing third parties to move tokens on behalf of the owner. Comparison: Basic Token vs. SAC Feature Basic Token SAC (Stellar Asset Contract) Standards Custom Soroban standard Decimals Built-in only Full decimal support Approvals Not included Built-in allowances Admin None Admin actions (freeze, clawback) Production Ready No Yes Learning Value High N/A For production systems, use SAC. This pattern is ideal for learning and prototyping. Deploy to Testnet​ Generate or use an existing account: soroban keys generate token-admin Fund your account via the Stellar Testnet Faucet. Deploy the contract: soroban contract deploy \ --wasm target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/token_transfer.wasm \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin This returns a contract ID (e.g., CABC...). Interact with the contract: soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- mint \ --to $(soroban keys address token-admin) \ --amount 1000 Query Balance​ soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- balance \ --of $(soroban keys address token-admin) Transfer Tokens​ soroban contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --network testnet \ --source token-admin \ -- transfer \ --from $(soroban keys address token-admin) \ --to GBBD...your-recipient \ --amount 100 For more details, see the Deploy to Testnet guide.

Set up your Soroban development environment on Windows. This guide covers both WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) - the recommended approach - and native Windows installation.
documents.s:
title: Windows Environment Setup
description: Complete guide to setting up Soroban development on Windows with WSL 2.
sidebar_position: 2

documents.t: Aspect WSL 2 (Recommended) Native Windows Setup Complexity Moderate High Performance Excellent Good Compatibility Best (Linux-based) Limited Troubleshooting Easier More issues Recommended For Most developers Advanced users Recommendation: Use WSL 2 for the smoothest experience. Native Windows setup is more complex due to toolchain differences.

Before you begin, ensure you have: Windows 10 (Build 19041+) or Windows 11 - For WSL 2 support Administrator access - Required for WSL installation Internet connection - For downloading dependencies Disk space - At least 5GB free (WSL) or 3GB (native) RAM - Minimum 4GB (8GB+ recommended)

Open PowerShell as Administrator and run: wsl --install This command: Enables the WSL 2 feature Installs Ubuntu as the default Linux distribution Sets WSL 2 as the default version Expected output: Installing: Virtual Machine Platform Virtual Machine Platform has been installed. Installing: Windows Subsystem for Linux Windows Subsystem for Linux has been installed. Downloading: Ubuntu Installing: Ubuntu Ubuntu has been installed. Launching Ubuntu...

After installation, Ubuntu will launch. You'll be prompted to: Create a username (use lowercase, no spaces) Create a password (you'll need this for sudo commands) Example: Installing, this may take a few minutes... Please create a default UNIX user account. The username does not need to match your Windows user name. For more information visit: https://aka.ms/wsldocs Enter new UNIX username: soroban New password: •••••••• Retype new password: •••••••• passwd: password updated successfully Installation successful!
Inside the WSL terminal, update your system: sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade -y
Install essential development packages: sudo apt install -y build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev curl git

Download and install Rust: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh When prompted, select the default installation option by pressing Enter. Load Rust into your current session: source $HOME/.cargo/env Verify installation: rustc --version cargo --version
Install using Cargo: cargo install --locked soroban-cli This may take several minutes. Verify installation: soroban --version
Add the WebAssembly target: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown Verify: rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown
Your Windows drives are automatically mounted in WSL. Access them via: # Navigate to Windows home directory cd /mnt/c/Users/YourUsername # Or use the shortcut cd ~

WSL 2 installed: wsl --list --verbose shows Ubuntu with version 2 Ubuntu updated: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y completes Rust installed: rustc --version returns a version number Cargo installed: cargo --version returns a version number Soroban CLI installed: soroban --version returns a version number WebAssembly target: rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown shows (installed) Git installed: git --version returns a version number VS Code Remote WSL extension installed (optional but recommended)

WSL Installation Fails​ Problem: Error: The system cannot find the file specified or installation hangs Solution: # Ensure you're running PowerShell as Administrator # Check Windows version [System.Environment]::OSVersion.Version # Should be 10.0.19041 or higher for WSL 2 # If older, update Windows first # Try manual installation wsl --install -d Ubuntu WSL 2 Not Available​ Problem: Error: WSL 2 requires an update to its kernel component Solution: # Download and install WSL 2 kernel update # Visit: https://aka.ms/wsl2kernel # After installation, set WSL 2 as default wsl --set-default-version 2 # Verify wsl --list --verbose Cannot Access Windows Files from WSL​ Problem: /mnt/c doesn't exist or is inaccessible Solution: # Check if mount exists ls /mnt # If not present, restart WSL wsl --shutdown # Then reopen WSL terminal Rust Installation Fails in WSL​ Problem: error: could not compile 'soroban-cli' Solution: # Update build tools sudo apt update sudo apt install -y build-essential pkg-config libssl-dev # Clean and retry cargo clean cargo install --locked soroban-cli -v Slow Performance in WSL​ Problem: Commands are slow, especially file operations Solution: # Store projects in WSL filesystem, not Windows # Good: ~/soroban-projects # Avoid: /mnt/c/Users/... # Check disk usage df -h # If full, clean up cargo clean

Rust Installation Fails​ Problem: error: Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or greater is required Solution: Download Build Tools for Visual Studio from visualstudio.microsoft.com Run installer and select "Desktop development with C++" Complete installation Restart PowerShell and retry Rust installation Soroban CLI Installation Hangs​ Problem: cargo install soroban-cli takes too long or times out Solution: # Try with verbose output cargo install --locked soroban-cli -v # Check internet connection Test-NetConnection -ComputerName github.com -Port 443 # If network is slow, try again later PATH Issues - Commands Not Found​ Problem: soroban: The term 'soroban' is not recognized Solution: # Check if Cargo bin is in PATH $env:PATH -split ';' | Select-String 'cargo' # If not present, add it manually $CargoPath = "$env:USERPROFILE\.cargo\bin" [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("PATH", "$env:PATH;$CargoPath", "User") # Restart PowerShell for changes to take effect Line Ending Issues​ Problem: Scripts fail with ^M characters or "bad interpreter" errors Solution: # Configure Git to handle line endings git config --global core.autocrlf true # For existing repositories git config core.autocrlf true # Convert existing files git add --renormalize . git commit -m "Normalize line endings" Permission Denied Errors​ Problem: Permission denied when running scripts Solution: # Check execution policy Get-ExecutionPolicy # If Restricted, change it Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser # For scripts in current directory Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope Process Build Fails with "linker not found"​ Problem: error: linker 'cc' not found or similar Solution: # Ensure Build Tools are installed # Download from: https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/downloads/ # Verify installation rustc --version --verbose # Should show MSVC version information

Line Ending Conflicts​ Problem: Files have different line endings on Windows vs WSL Solution: # In WSL, configure Git git config --global core.autocrlf input # In PowerShell, configure Git git config --global core.autocrlf true # This ensures consistent line endings across platforms Antivirus Interference​ Problem: Installation is slow or fails intermittently Solution: Add your project directory to antivirus exclusions Temporarily disable antivirus during installation Check antivirus logs for blocked operations Disk Space Issues​ Problem: No space left on device during installation Solution: # Check available space Get-Volume # Clean up # Delete old Rust toolchains rustup toolchain list rustup toolchain uninstall <old-version> # Clean Cargo cache cargo clean

In Soroban, types are more than just data containers—they define the contract's storage footprint, gas efficiency, and long-term maintainability. This guide covers strategies for designing custom types that are robust, efficient, and evolvable. Why Type Design Matters Smart contracts are immutable by nature, but their state persists across upgrades. Poorly designed types can lead to "storage bloat," high gas costs for reads/writes, and complex migrations when business requirements change.
When translating domain concepts (like "User Account" or "Liquidity Pool") into contract types, you must decide how to represent them in storage.

Value Objects: Types defined by their attributes (e.g., Amount, Price). In Soroban, these are usually small structs or newtype wrappers. Entities: Types with a unique identity that persists over time (e.g., User, Proposal). These are typically stored as large structs keyed by a unique ID or Address.

Use the "Newtype" pattern to wrap primitive types. This prevents accidental confusion between different units or IDs that share the same underlying type. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct OrderId(pub u32); #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct TokenId(pub u32); // Compiler will prevent passing a TokenId where an OrderId is expected pub fn get_order(env: Env, id: OrderId) { ... }
Soroban uses a highly optimized serialization format (XDR). To make a custom type usable in a contract, it must be annotated with #[contracttype].

Structs: For grouping related data. Enums: For representing state or mutually exclusive options. Prims: i128, u32, Address, Bytes, Symbol, etc. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum ContractState { Active, Paused, Upgrading(u32), // Enums can carry data } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct Order { pub id: OrderId, pub owner: Address, pub amount: i128, pub status: ContractState, }
Every byte stored in the ledger costs gas. Serialization size directly impacts the read_ledger_entry and write_ledger_entry costs.

Prefer Small Primitives: Use u32 or u64 instead of i128 if the value range allows. Avoid Unnecessary Strings: Use Symbol for short, fixed strings (up to 32 characters). They are significantly cheaper than String. Flat vs. Nested: Highly nested structs increase serialization complexity. Keep storage types as flat as possible. Bit-Packing (Advanced): For extremely high-frequency operations, consider packing multiple booleans or small integers into a single u64. Read/Write Amplification Reading a 1KB struct to change a single boolean field still costs the gas for a 1KB read. If a struct grows too large, consider splitting it into separate storage keys.

Use enums to manage the lifecycle of a contract or entity. This makes illegal transitions impossible at the type level. #[contracttype] pub enum ProposalStatus { Pending, Voting { start_time: u64, end_time: u64 }, Executed, Expired, } pub fn cast_vote(env: Env, id: u32) -> Result<(), Error> { let proposal = get_proposal(&env, id)?; match proposal.status { ProposalStatus::Voting { start_time, end_time } => { let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); if now < start_time || now > end_time { return Err(Error::VotingNotActive); } // Proceed with voting... } _ => return Err(Error::InvalidStatus), } Ok(()) }

Group global contract settings into a single struct. This is more efficient than storing 10 separate configuration variables in 10 different storage keys. #[contracttype] pub struct Config { pub admin: Address, pub fee_bps: u32, pub min_deposit: i128, } impl Config { pub fn get(env: &Env) -> Self { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Config).unwrap() } }
Never trust data coming into the contract. Validate types at the entry point (contractimpl).

Range Checks: Ensure amounts are positive and within expected bounds. Sanitization: Check that Address types aren't the null address if applicable. State Invariants: Verify that the internal state of a struct is consistent (e.g., start_time < end_time). pub fn create_order(env: Env, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // ... }
As your project grows, you may need to add fields to your structs. Because storage is persistent, you must handle "schema drift."

Instead of storing a raw struct, store an enum that wraps different versions of the data. #[contracttype] pub enum AccountState { V1(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV1 { pub balance: i128, } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV2 { pub balance: i128, pub rewards_points: u64, // New field added in V2 } // Lazy Migration pub fn get_account(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { // Upgrade V1 to V2 on the fly AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards_points: 0, } } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Integer Overflows: Always use checked math (checked_add, checked_mul) when performing calculations on numeric types. Unbounded Collections: Avoid using Vec or Map in storage types if they can grow indefinitely. This can lead to "gas exhaustion" attacks where reading the state becomes impossible. Type Confusion: Use Symbol or OrderId wrappers to ensure you aren't using a user-provided integer to index into the wrong data structure.

All custom types are annotated with #[contracttype]. Enums are used to represent state and avoid "boolean soup." Newtype wrappers protect against ID/unit confusion. Large structs are evaluated for potential splitting to save gas. A migration strategy (like Versioned State) is planned for future updates. Inputs are validated at the contract boundary.
Set up your Soroban development environment on macOS. This guide covers Intel and Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) Macs running macOS 11 (Big Sur) or later.

Before you begin, ensure you have: macOS 11 (Big Sur) or later - Both Intel and Apple Silicon supported Xcode Command Line Tools - Required for compilation Homebrew - Package manager for macOS Rust - Latest stable version Soroban CLI - Command-line interface for Soroban Code Editor - VS Code or your preferred editor Git - Version control (included with Xcode)

RAM: Minimum 2GB (4GB+ recommended) Disk Space: At least 3GB free space Internet: Required for downloading dependencies Apple Silicon Note: Most tools now have native M1/M2/M3 support, but some may need Rosetta 2

Xcode Command Line Tools provide essential build tools and Git. These are required before installing Rust and other dependencies. Check if already installed: xcode-select --version If not installed, install using: xcode-select --install A dialog box will appear. Click "Install" and wait for completion (this may take 10-15 minutes). Verify installation: gcc --version make --version git --version All commands should return version information.

Homebrew is macOS's package manager, making it easy to install development tools. Install Homebrew by running: /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" Apple Silicon Users: After installation, add Homebrew to your PATH by adding the following line to your shell profile (~/.zprofile or ~/.bashrc): export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" Reload your shell: source ~/.zprofile # or source ~/.bashrc Intel Mac Users: Homebrew installs to /usr/local/bin which is already in your PATH. Verify installation: brew --version
Some Rust packages benefit from system-provided OpenSSL: brew install openssl

Use Homebrew to install Rust (simplest method for macOS): brew install rust Alternatively, use rustup (official Rust installer) for more control: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh When prompted, select the default installation option by pressing Enter. Load Rust into your current session: source $HOME/.cargo/env Verify installation: rustc --version cargo --version Both commands should return version numbers.

Install the Soroban CLI using Cargo: cargo install --locked soroban-cli This may take several minutes as it compiles from source. For Apple Silicon, this will compile native binaries. Verify installation: soroban --version

Add the WebAssembly target to your Rust toolchain: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown Verify the target was added: rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown You should see wasm32-unknown-unknown (installed).
Create a workspace directory for your Soroban projects: mkdir -p ~/soroban-projects cd ~/soroban-projects

Run this comprehensive verification to ensure everything is installed correctly: echo "=== Xcode Command Line Tools Verification ===" xcode-select --version gcc --version echo "=== Homebrew Verification ===" brew --version echo "=== Rust Verification ===" rustc --version cargo --version echo "=== Soroban CLI Verification ===" soroban --version echo "=== WebAssembly Target Verification ===" rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown echo "=== Git Verification ===" git --version All commands should return version information without errors.

Use this checklist to confirm your environment is ready: Xcode Command Line Tools: xcode-select --version returns a version number Homebrew installed: brew --version returns a version number Rust installed: rustc --version returns a version number Cargo installed: cargo --version returns a version number Soroban CLI installed: soroban --version returns a version number WebAssembly target available: rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown shows (installed) Git installed: git --version returns a version number Internet connectivity: curl https://www.google.com succeeds

Most development tools now have native Apple Silicon support. Homebrew automatically installs native binaries when available. Check your architecture: uname -m Returns arm64 = Apple Silicon (native) Returns x86_64 = Intel or Rosetta 2
Homebrew typically handles this automatically. If you need to force native installation: # Remove and reinstall with native binaries brew uninstall rust brew install rust
If Homebrew installed to /opt/homebrew/bin and tools aren't found, add to your shell profile: # Add to ~/.zprofile or ~/.bashrc export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" Then reload: source ~/.zprofile

Installation Fails or Hangs​ Problem: xcode-select --install doesn't open dialog or hangs Solution: # Try removing and reinstalling sudo rm -rf /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools xcode-select --install # Or download directly from Apple # Visit: https://developer.apple.com/download/ # Check installation path xcode-select -p # Should return: /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools "Can't find package to install" Error​ Problem: Dialog shows "Can't find package to install" Solution: # Accept Xcode license sudo xcode-select --reset sudo xcodebuild -license accept # Then try installation again xcode-select --install

documents.t: Homebrew Installation Fails​ Problem: curl command fails or installation hangs Solution: # Check internet connection ping -c 3 apple.com # Try alternative installation method ruby -e "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/master/install)" # Or visit https://brew.sh for latest instructions M1/M2 Homebrew in Wrong Location​ Problem: Homebrew installed to /usr/local instead of /opt/homebrew Solution: # Check Homebrew location which brew # If in /usr/local, uninstall and reinstall /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/uninstall.sh)" # Then reinstall /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" # Add to PATH if needed echo 'export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zprofile source ~/.zprofile "Permission Denied" When Installing Packages​ Problem: brew install returns permission error Solution: # Check Homebrew directory ownership ls -la /usr/local/Cellar # Fix permissions sudo chown -R $(whoami) /usr/local/Cellar sudo chown -R $(whoami) /usr/local/bin # Or reinstall Homebrew with correct permissions /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/uninstall.sh)" /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Rust Installation via Homebrew Fails​ Problem: brew install rust fails or is slow Solution: # Try official rustup installer instead curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh # Then reload shell source $HOME/.cargo/env # Verify rustc --version "Command Not Found: rustc"​ Problem: rustc: command not found after installation Solution: # Source Rust environment source $HOME/.cargo/env # Add to shell profile to persist echo 'source $HOME/.cargo/env' >> ~/.zprofile # Reload shell source ~/.zprofile # Verify rustc --version M1/M2 Rust Compilation Slow​ Problem: Building Rust projects takes very long on Apple Silicon Solution: # Ensure you have native toolchain rustup target list | grep wasm32-unknown-unknown # Should show: wasm32-unknown-unknown (installed) # Update toolchain rustup update # Clean and rebuild cargo clean cargo build --release

Soroban Installation Hangs or Times Out​ Problem: cargo install --locked soroban-cli takes too long or times out Solution: # Try with verbose output cargo install --locked soroban-cli -v # Check internet connection ping -c 3 github.com # If network is slow, try again later or use: cargo install --locked soroban-cli --version 20.0.0 "Soroban Command Not Found"​ Problem: soroban: command not found Solution: # Check if Cargo bin is in PATH echo $PATH | grep cargo # If not, add it echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zprofile source ~/.zprofile # Verify soroban --version Build Fails with Linker Error​ Problem: error: linker 'cc' not found or similar Solution: # Ensure Xcode Command Line Tools are installed xcode-select --install # Verify installation gcc --version # Try installation again cargo install --locked soroban-cli

Tools Installed but Not Found​ Problem: Commands like rustc or soroban not found despite installation Solution: # Check your shell echo $SHELL # For zsh (default on macOS 10.15+) # Add to ~/.zprofile: export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$PATH" # For M1/M2 # For bash # Add to ~/.bash_profile or ~/.bashrc: export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" export PATH="/usr/local/bin:$PATH" # For Intel # Reload configuration source ~/.zprofile # or source ~/.bash_profile Multiple Rust Installations Conflict​ Problem: Both Homebrew and rustup Rust installed, causing conflicts Solution: # Remove Homebrew version brew uninstall rust # Use only rustup version # Verify rustc --version which rustc # Should return ~/.cargo/bin/rustc

SSL Certificate Verification Failed​ Problem: SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED when downloading dependencies Solution: # Update CA certificates (usually automatic on macOS) # If issue persists, try: /Applications/Python\ 3.x/Install\ Certificates.command # Or update Git brew install git # Try installation again cargo install --locked soroban-cli

"No Space Left on Device" Error​ Problem: Installation fails due to insufficient disk space Solution: # Check available space df -h # Clean up Cargo cache cargo clean # Remove old Rust toolchains rustup toolchain list rustup toolchain uninstall <old-toolchain> # Clean Homebrew cache brew cleanup

VS Code Rust Analyzer Issues​ Problem: Rust analyzer not working in VS Code Solution: Install "Rust-analyzer" extension in VS Code Install "CodeLLDB" extension for debugging Reload VS Code Check that Rust path is correct: # In VS Code Terminal which rustc which cargo VS Code Terminal Doesn't See Tools​ Problem: Terminal in VS Code can't find rustc or soroban Solution: Close VS Code completely Open terminal and verify tools work: rustc --version Reopen VS Code Open integrated terminal (Ctrl+`) Tools should now be available If still not working, add to VS Code settings: "terminal.integrated.inheritEnv": true

Create a dedicated terminal profile for Soroban development: # Open ~/.zprofile (or ~/.bash_profile for bash) nano ~/.zprofile # Add these lines at the end: export SOROBAN_RPC_HOST="http://localhost:8000" export SOROBAN_NETWORK_PASSPHRASE="Test SDF Network ; September 2015" # Save and reload source ~/.zprofile
# Use all CPU cores for building cargo build --release -j $(sysctl -n hw.ncpu) # Or set in Cargo.toml [profile.release] codegen-units = 1 lto = true
# Use cargo-tree to understand dependencies cargo install cargo-tree cargo tree # Check build times cargo build -v # Profile compilation cargo build -v --timings

The contract factory pattern enables dynamic deployment of multiple contract instances from a single factory contract. This is useful for creating standardized contracts at runtime without manual deployment.

A factory contract acts as a centralized deployer that can: Deploy child contract instances on-demand Track all deployed instances Initialize child contracts with custom parameters Manage the lifecycle of multiple contracts

Token Issuance: Deploy a new token contract for each asset User Accounts: Create individual contract instances for user-specific logic Multi-tenancy: Deploy isolated instances for different organizations Pool Management: Create liquidity pools dynamically Marketplace: Deploy individual shop contracts from a marketplace factory

The factory pattern typically consists of: Factory Contract: Manages deployment and tracking Child Contract: The template contract that gets deployed multiple times Registry: Maintains a list of deployed instances Factory Contract ├── deploy_child(name) ├── get_deployed_children() └── child_count() Child Contract (Template) ├── init(name) ├── get_name() └── get_info()

The child contract is the template that will be deployed multiple times: #[contract] pub struct ChildContract; #[contractimpl] impl ChildContract { pub fn init(env: Env, name: Symbol) { env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("name"), &name); } pub fn get_name(env: Env) -> Symbol { env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")) } pub fn get_info(env: Env) -> (Symbol, Address) { let name = env .storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")); let contract_id = env.current_contract_address(); (name, contract_id) } }

The factory deploys and tracks child instances: #[contract] pub struct ContractFactory; #[contractimpl] impl ContractFactory { pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { // Get child contract code let child_code = env.deployer().get_programm_id(&symbol_short!("child")); // Generate unique salt for deterministic deployment let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .temporary() .set(&(), &(salt + 1)); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec(); // Deploy new instance let child_address = env .deployer() .deploy_contract( &salt_bytes, &child_code, Address::from_contract_id(&env.current_contract_address()) ); // Track deployed contract let mut deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.push_back(child_address.clone()); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&symbol_short!("deployed"), &deployed); child_address } pub fn get_deployed_children(env: Env) -> Vec<Address> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]) } pub fn child_count(env: Env) -> u32 { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.len() as u32 } }

The factory pattern includes comprehensive tests: #[test] fn test_factory_deploy_multiple_children() { let env = Env::default(); let factory_contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ContractFactory); let factory_client = ContractFactoryClient::new(&env, &factory_contract_id); // Deploy multiple children let child1 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-1")); let child2 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-2")); let child3 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-3")); // Verify all are tracked assert_eq!(factory_client.child_count(), 3); let deployed = factory_client.get_deployed_children(); assert_eq!(deployed.len(), 3); assert!(deployed.contains(&child1)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child2)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child3)); }
Use unique salts to ensure different deployment addresses: let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec();
Persistent storage: For tracking important metadata Temporary storage: For non-critical counters Instance storage: For child contract-specific data
Always initialize child contracts with necessary parameters: client.init(&name);
Maintain a registry of deployed instances for: Verification Monitoring Upgrade coordination Access control

Pass parameters when deploying: pub fn deploy_child_with_params( env: Env, name: Symbol, owner: Address, config: Config, ) -> Address { // Deploy let child_address = /* deployment logic */; // Initialize with parameters let client = ChildContractClient::new(&env, &child_address); client.init(&name); // ... set owner, config, etc child_address }

Restrict who can deploy: pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { let caller = env.invoker(); let authorized: Address = env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&caller); require!(caller == authorized, Error::NotAuthorized); // Deploy logic... }

Retrieve specific child contracts: pub fn get_child_by_index(env: Env, index: u32) -> Address { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.get(index as usize) }

This pattern guide defines a comprehensive error handling methodology for Soroban smart contracts. It covers establishing a clear error taxonomy, implementing custom error patterns, executing propagation strategies, and ensuring user-facing clarity. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed Basic understanding of Rust's Result type and enum definitions Familiarity with the soroban_sdk environment Error Taxonomy and Custom Patterns A well-defined error taxonomy categorizes errors into logical groups. This prevents overlapping error codes, aids debugging, and makes client-side handling predictable. Common Taxonomy Categories​ Validation Errors (100-199): Invalid inputs, out of bounds, incorrect formats. Authorization Errors (200-299): Missing signatures, unauthorized roles. State Errors (300-399): Invalid state transitions, uninitialized data. Resource Errors (400-499): Insufficient balance, out of gas. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { // Validation Errors (100+) InvalidAmount = 101, InvalidAddress = 102, // Authorization Errors (200+) Unauthorized = 201, RoleNotFound = 202, // State Errors (300+) AlreadyInitialized = 301, NotInitialized = 302, // Resource Errors (400+) InsufficientBalance = 401, InsufficientAllowance = 402, } #[contract] pub struct TokenContract; #[contractimpl] impl TokenContract { pub fn transfer( env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let balance = env.storage().persistent().get(&from).unwrap_or(0); if balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Execute transfer logic here (simplified for example) let new_balance = balance - amount; env.storage().persistent().set(&from, &new_balance); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_taxonomy_errors() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // Test Validation Error (100-199 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-10); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test Resource Error (400-499 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); } } Propagation and Handling Strategies Using the ? operator allows you to gracefully propagate errors up the call stack. This pattern advocates breaking complex operations into smaller, isolated functions that validate conditions or calculate state and return a Result. Why Propagate? Propagating errors rather than panicking ensures that your contract gracefully halts and provides exact error reasons to the caller, preventing unknown execution states. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum WorkflowError { InvalidInput = 1, ProcessingFailed = 2, } #[contract] pub struct WorkflowContract; #[contractimpl] impl WorkflowContract { pub fn complex_workflow(env: Env, user: Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { user.require_auth(); // Strategy: Delegate and propagate errors using '?' Self::validate_input(&env, value)?; Self::process_data(&env, &user, value)?; Ok(()) } fn validate_input(_env: &Env, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { if value < 0 { return Err(WorkflowError::InvalidInput); } Ok(()) } fn process_data(env: &Env, user: &Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { // Business logic that could fail if value == 42 { return Err(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed); } env.storage().persistent().set(user, &value); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_error_propagation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, WorkflowContract); let client = WorkflowContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // The error naturally propagates from validate_input up to the contract entrypoint let result_validation = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &-5); assert_eq!(result_validation, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::InvalidInput))); // The error propagates from process_data up to the contract entrypoint let result_processing = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &42); assert_eq!(result_processing, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed))); } } User-Facing Clarity Recommendations To ensure frontend clients and indexers can clearly interpret contract failures, implement these recommendations: Standardize Error Codes: Publicly document your error taxonomy in your repository (e.g., in a README or developer portal). Clients rely on these numerical codes. Emit Telemetry Events: For critical path failures, emit an event before returning an error. This aids indexing services in tracking exact failure reasons. Use Descriptive Enums: Naming your Rust enum variants clearly translates to easier debugging when using the Soroban CLI or SDK tools. Provide Client-Side Mapping: Create an SDK or frontend utility mapping the numeric u32 error codes to human-readable messages (e.g., 101 -> "The requested token amount is invalid"). Event Emission on Failure Remember that if a contract returns an error, the transaction rolls back, and any events emitted during that invocation are dropped. Therefore, telemetry events for failures only work if you catch the error at a higher level or in a parent contract. In the world of immutable ledgers, contract upgrades are among the most sensitive operations a developer can perform. A mistake in an upgrade can result in permanent loss of state, locked funds, or protocol insolvency. This guide treats contract upgrades as high-risk, irreversible operations requiring rigorous governance and verification. Safety First Always simulate upgrades and migrations on a local sandbox or testnet before executing on mainnet. Once state is corrupted on-chain, recovery is often impossible.
A healthy protocol moves through distinct phases, each with specific entry and exit criteria.
Criteria: Code is feature-complete and passes all unit/integration tests. Action: Internal or external security audit of the Wasm bytecode and source logic. Exit: No high-severity issues remain.

Criteria: Deployment of the exact audited bytecode to a live network environment. Action: Manual QA, integration testing with front-end, and "chaos testing" (e.g., simulating high load). Exit: Contract behaves as expected in a multi-user environment.
Criteria: Final verification of initialization arguments and governance keys. Action: Atomic deployment and initialization. Exit: Success events emitted; state invariants verified.
Criteria: Ongoing operation. Action: Monitoring events, transaction volume, and potential anomalies. Exit: Identification of a bug or requirement for a feature upgrade.

Criteria: A newer version is ready or the feature is sunset. Action: "Sunset" phase where new deposits are disabled but withdrawals remain open. Exit: All funds removed; storage entries deleted where possible.

Upgrades must be protected by strict access control. In Soroban, the upgrade function should typically require the authorization of an admin or a decentralized governance body. #[contractimpl] impl MyContract { pub fn upgrade(env: Env, new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>) { let admin: Address = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); admin.require_auth(); // Ensure only the authorized admin can upgrade env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash); } } Governance Best Practice For high-value protocols, avoid single-key admin accounts. Use a multi-signature account or a DAO with a mandatory timelock (e.g., 7 days) to allow users to exit if they disagree with a pending upgrade.
Soroban provides native support for updating contract logic while preserving the contract ID and storage.

The most common way to upgrade is to call env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(). This replaces the contract's executable code with the bytecode associated with the provided Wasm hash. Use when: You need to fix a bug or add features without changing the contract's address. Avoid when: You need to change the fundamental architecture or storage model in a way that is incompatible with existing state. See the tested upgradeable example for a complete admin-gated upgrade flow with storage preservation and integration tests.
When you upgrade logic, you often need to evolve the data structures in storage.

Upgrade individual storage entries only when they are accessed. This spreads the gas cost over many transactions and avoids hitting gas limits. #[contracttype] pub enum AccountState { V1(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } pub fn get_account_v2(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { let upgraded = AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards: 0, // Initialize new field }; // Save the upgraded state back to storage env.storage().persistent().set(&user, &AccountState::V2(upgraded.clone())); upgraded } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Perform the entire migration in a single transaction or a series of transactions. Risk: High gas consumption. May fail if the dataset is too large. Best for: Small, fixed-size datasets (e.g., global configuration).

Bytecode hash of the new Wasm is verified. New storage types are backward-compatible (or migration is planned). Initialization logic for new fields is tested. Upgrade transaction has been simulated on a Testnet fork. Governance keys are active and accessible.
Smoke tests pass (basic deposits/withdrawals). State invariants remain valid (e.g., Total Supply = sum of Balances). Version markers in storage have been updated. Events are being emitted correctly.

If an upgrade introduces a critical flaw, you must have a plan to recover. Immutable Fallback: If the contract is truly immutable, you cannot upgrade. Your only "rollback" is to deploy a new contract and ask users to migrate. Logic Rollback: Call upgrade again with the hash of the previous stable Wasm bytecode. Emergency Pause: Include a "Circuit Breaker" to halt operations while you diagnose and fix a failed upgrade. See the tested emergency-stop example for a minimal, admin-gated pause()/unpause() implementation with a fail_if_paused guard applied to operational entry points.

I have a clearly defined lifecycle for my contract. My upgrade function is protected by require_auth. I have chosen between Lazy and Eager migration for state changes. I have a verified rollback procedure. I have completed the pre-upgrade checklist on Testnet.

Governance contracts need a clear, auditable state machine so that proposals can only advance through valid transitions. This pattern encodes the full lifecycle as a #[contracttype] enum and enforces transitions at the contract boundary, making invalid states unrepresentable on-chain. Pending ──► Active ──► Succeeded ──► Executed └──► Defeated Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Familiarity with contracttype enums and instance storage Implementation Design principle Encode every invalid state as a compile-time impossibility or a guarded assert!. Never rely on callers to pass the right state — the contract should enforce it. Contract Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env}; /// All valid proposal states. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Debug)] pub enum ProposalState { Pending, // created but voting not open Active, // voting is open Succeeded, // more for-votes than against Defeated, // equal or more against-votes Executed, // on-chain action has been carried out } #[contracttype] pub enum DataKey { State, VotesFor, VotesAgainst, } #[contract] pub struct SimpleDao; #[contractimpl] impl SimpleDao { /// Create a new proposal in the Pending state. pub fn create(env: Env) { env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Pending); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &0_u32); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &0_u32); } /// Pending → Active: open voting. pub fn activate(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Pending, "must be Pending to activate"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Active); } /// Record a vote while Active. pub fn vote(env: Env, in_favor: bool) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "voting is not open"); if in_favor { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &(v + 1)); } else { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &(v + 1)); } } /// Active → Succeeded or Defeated based on vote counts. pub fn finalize(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "must be Active to finalize"); let for_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); let against_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); let next = if for_votes > against_votes { ProposalState::Succeeded } else { ProposalState::Defeated }; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &next); } /// Succeeded → Executed: carry out the on-chain action. pub fn execute(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Succeeded, "must be Succeeded to execute"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Executed); } pub fn get_state(env: Env) -> ProposalState { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap() } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::Env; fn setup() -> (Env, soroban_sdk::Address) { let env = Env::default(); let id = env.register(SimpleDao, ()); (env, id) } #[test] fn test_create_sets_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Pending); } #[test] fn test_pending_to_active() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Active); } #[test] fn test_active_to_succeeded() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Succeeded); } #[test] fn test_active_to_defeated() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Defeated); } #[test] fn test_succeeded_to_executed() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); client.execute(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Executed); } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Pending to activate")] fn test_cannot_activate_twice() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.activate(); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "voting is not open")] fn test_cannot_vote_when_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.vote(&true); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Succeeded to execute")] fn test_cannot_execute_defeated_proposal() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); client.execute(); // invalid } } Security considerations Authorization: Production DAOs must guard activate, finalize, and execute with require_auth() on a governor address or multi-sig. The example omits this for clarity. Tie handling: The current rule (for > against) treats ties as defeats. Make this explicit in your governance spec. Double execution: Once Executed, the state cannot regress. Add any further idempotency guards inside the execute body. Sybil resistance: Vote weighting (token-weighted, NFT-gated) must be added before production use. Production checklist Add require_auth() guards on every privileged transition before deploying to mainnet. } else { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &(v + 1)); } } /// Active → Succeeded or Defeated based on vote counts. pub fn finalize(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "must be Active to finalize"); let for_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); let against_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); let next = if for_votes > against_votes { ProposalState::Succeeded } else { ProposalState::Defeated }; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &next); } /// Succeeded → Executed: carry out the on-chain action. pub fn execute(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Succeeded, "must be Succeeded to execute"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Executed); } pub fn get_state(env: Env) -> ProposalState { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap() } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Pending); } #[test] fn test_pending_to_active() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Active); } #[test] fn test_active_to_succeeded() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Succeeded); } #[test] fn test_active_to_defeated() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Defeated); } #[test] fn test_succeeded_to_executed() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); client.execute(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Executed); } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Pending to activate")] fn test_cannot_activate_twice() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.activate(); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "voting is not open")] fn test_cannot_vote_when_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.vote(&true); // invalid } #[test] #[should_panic(expected = "must be Succeeded to execute")] fn test_cannot_execute_defeated_proposal() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); client.execute(); // invalid } }

Authorization: Production DAOs must guard activate, finalize, and execute with require_auth() on a governor address or multi-sig. The example omits this for clarity. Tie handling: The current rule (for > against) treats ties as defeats. Make this explicit in your governance spec. Double execution: Once Executed, the state cannot regress. Add any further idempotency guards inside the execute body. Sybil resistance: Vote weighting (token-weighted, NFT-gated) must be added before production use. Production checklist Add require_auth() guards on every privileged transition before deploying to mainnet.

The oracle consumer pattern enables smart contracts to read external data (price feeds, asset prices, etc.) from trusted oracle contracts through cross-contract invocation.

An oracle consumer contract: Reads data from an external oracle contract Validates data freshness and accuracy Uses prices for calculations (value estimation, collateral checks) Handles oracle failures gracefully Maintains configurable trust parameters

DEX/AMM: Price feeds for token swaps and liquidity pools Lending Protocols: Collateral valuation and liquidation pricing Staking: Asset price feeds for reward calculations Insurance: Event triggers based on oracle data Derivatives: Price feeds for options and futures

┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Oracle Consumer Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ get_price(asset) │ │ get_price_data(asset) │ │ calculate_value(asset, amt) │ │ validate_freshness() │ └──────────┬──────────────────┘ │ Cross-Contract Call │ ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐ │ Oracle Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ price_feeds (persistent) │ │ last_update (timestamp) │ │ update_prices() │ └─────────────────────────────┘

Query: Consumer asks oracle for price of asset Fetch: Oracle looks up price from data store Return: Oracle returns price with metadata (decimals, timestamp) Validate: Consumer checks freshness and accuracy Use: Consumer uses validated price for calculations
Oracle Contract: Deployed by trusted party Data Accuracy: Oracle is incentivized to provide accurate prices Timeliness: Oracle updates prices regularly Integrity: Oracle cannot be tampered with

Freshness Checks: Reject stale data beyond max_age Price Bounds: Reject prices outside reasonable ranges Multiple Oracles: Average prices from multiple sources Circuit Breakers: Pause operations if prices are unusual

#[contract] pub struct OracleConsumer; #[contractimpl] impl OracleConsumer { /// Initialize with oracle address and data freshness requirement pub fn init(env: Env, oracle_address: Address, max_age_secs: u64) { env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &oracle_address); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("max_age"), &max_age_secs); } /// Fetch price from oracle with validation pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let oracle = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("oracle")) .expect("Oracle not initialized"); // Call oracle contract let price_data: Vec<i128> = env .invoke_contract( &oracle, &symbol_short!("get_price"), soroban_sdk::vec![&env, asset.into_val(&env)], ) .map_err(|_| OracleError::InvalidOracle)?; // Validate response format if price_data.len() < 3 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } let price = price_data.get_unchecked(0); let timestamp = price_data.get_unchecked(2) as u64; // Validate price is positive if price <= 0 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } // Check data freshness let max_age = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("max_age")) .unwrap_or(3600); let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); let age = current_time.checked_sub(timestamp) .ok_or(OracleError::StaleData)?; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); } Ok(price) } /// Calculate value of amount based on oracle price pub fn calculate_value( env: Env, asset: Symbol, amount: i128, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let (price, decimals, _) = self.get_price_data(env, asset)?; // value = (amount * price) / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) } }

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum OracleError { StaleData = 1, // Data too old InvalidOracle = 2, // Oracle call failed InvalidPrice = 3, // Price is invalid Unauthorized = 4, // Not authorized }

The oracle consumer includes comprehensive tests with a mock oracle: #[contract] pub struct MockOracle; #[contractimpl] impl MockOracle { pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Vec<i128> { // Return: [price, decimals, timestamp] soroban_sdk::vec![ &env, 1_000_000, // $1.00 6, // 6 decimals env.ledger().timestamp() as i128, // current time ] } } #[test] fn test_get_price() { let env = Env::default(); let consumer_id = env.register_contract(None, OracleConsumer); let oracle_id = env.register_contract(None, MockOracle); let client = OracleConsumerClient::new(&env, &consumer_id); client.init(&oracle_id, &3600); let price = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")).unwrap(); assert_eq!(price, 1_000_000); } #[test] fn test_stale_data_rejection() { let env = Env::default(); // ... setup ... // Advance time beyond max_age env.ledger_mut().set_timestamp(old_timestamp + 7200); let result = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")); assert_eq!(result, Err(OracleError::StaleData)); }
Always validate timestamp and reject stale data: let max_age = 3600; // 1 hour let age = current_time - timestamp; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); }
Reject prices outside reasonable ranges: // BTC price between $10k and $100k if price < 10_000_000_000 || price > 100_000_000_000 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); }

Use multiple oracles to prevent single point of failure: pub fn get_median_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let mut prices = Vec::new(); for oracle_addr in self.get_oracles(&env)? { if let Ok(price) = self.fetch_from_oracle(&env, &oracle_addr, &asset) { prices.push(price); } } if prices.is_empty() { return Err(OracleError::InvalidOracle); } // Return median to handle outliers prices.sort(); Ok(prices[prices.len() / 2]) }

Handle oracle failures gracefully: pub fn get_price_or_cached( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Try fresh price match self.get_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { // Cache for fallback self.cache_price(&env, &asset, price)?; Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Fall back to cached price if oracle fails self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset) } } }

Restrict configuration changes to authorized addresses: pub fn set_oracle(env: Env, new_oracle: Address) { let admin: Address = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&admin); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &new_oracle); }

Handle different decimal places: pub fn normalize_price(price: i128, decimals: u32, target_decimals: u32) -> i128 { if decimals > target_decimals { price / 10_i128.pow(decimals - target_decimals) } else { price * 10_i128.pow(target_decimals - decimals) } }

Calculate asset value from price and amount: pub fn calculate_usd_value( price: i128, // Price in USD decimals: u32, // Price decimals amount: i128, // Amount of asset amount_decimals: u32, // Asset decimals ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Normalize to same decimal place let price_normalized = normalize_price(price, decimals, amount_decimals); // value = amount * price / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price_normalized) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(amount_decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) }

Pause operations if price changes dramatically: pub fn check_circuit_breaker( env: Env, asset: Symbol, new_price: i128, ) -> Result<(), OracleError> { let old_price = self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset)?; // Allow max 20% price change let max_deviation = old_price / 5; let deviation = (new_price as i128 - old_price).abs(); if deviation > max_deviation { return Err(OracleError::PriceDeviation); } Ok(()) }

Risk: Oracle goes offline, contract uses stale prices Mitigation: Set reasonable max_age (typically 1 hour) Monitor oracle update frequency Use circuit breakers for unusual price changes Fall back to cached prices
Risk: Oracle provides false prices Mitigation: Use multiple independent oracle sources Verify oracle is properly incentivized/bonded Implement price bounds checking Monitor for suspicious patterns

Risk: Malicious oracle contract returns crafted data Mitigation: Whitelist oracle addresses Validate response format and types Use safe math (checked_mul, checked_div) Test with multiple data scenarios
Risk: Oracle takes excessive gas or fails unexpectedly Mitigation: Set gas limits on oracle calls Implement timeouts Use try/catch for failure scenarios Fall back to cached prices

Trust Dependency: Consumer trusts oracle's data accuracy Availability: Relies on oracle being online Latency: Data is never completely real-time Cost: Oracle calls consume gas Manipulation: Oracles can be attacked or compromised
